title: Every soul shall taste death
hookLine: every soul will taste of death (Quran 3:185)

lines: EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.
cards: A short line in Arabic: kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt. In Pickthall's old English translation of the Quran, it reads: "Every soul will taste of death."

It's short enough to carve on a stone or say at a graveside, and some Muslims do both. It sits in the third surah, the family of Imran, near a verse about being tested and holding on with patience. It doesn't argue.
It doesn't comfort, not yet. It just says what is going to happen, to everyone.

teach.h: NO SOUL IS LEFT OFF THE LIST.
teach.b: The Arabic word kull means each, all, every one. There's no list of exceptions. Elsewhere the Quran tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that no human before him was given life forever.
Every soul includes the strong and the weak, the well-known and the forgotten, the one reading the verse aloud. Then the verb. The Quran could have said every soul will die.
Instead it uses a word from the mouth: to taste. Some readers notice what that suggests: a taste is something you go through, and the one who tastes is still there afterward.
The verse goes on: you will be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is kept from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won.
For Muslims, death is not a wall at the end of the road.
It's a door, and past it lie accounting and mercy. The verse closes: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion."
In Muslim teaching this doesn't call the world worthless, since the Quran praises its good things too.
It warns not to mistake the borrowed for the lasting.
The same opening words come back in other surahs, and in surah twenty-nine they're followed at once by a return to God.

how: Muslims recite this verse in sermons and at funerals, and some families have it carved on gravestones; it is recalled when news of a death arrives, alongside the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

o: a walled courtyard where Muslims bury their dead
what the Quran promises those kept from the Fire after death
a quiet garden where pilgrims rest on the road to Mecca

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: when every soul is paid in full

s: the verse says only sinners will taste death
it says every soul, with no exceptions.
the next sentence speaks of the Day of Resurrection and the Garden.
the same words appear in more than one surah
they come back in surahs 21 and 29.

games.q: a verse tells you every soul will taste of death. what does it say next?
o: that you'll be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection.
that only some souls are counted.
games.why: the verse goes straight on to the Day of Resurrection: whoever is kept from the Fire and brought into the Garden has won.

practice: Let the words come once, slowly: every soul will taste of death.
Then, on each out-breath, let every soul be enough, every soul in this building, on this street, the people you love, the people you've never met, and you, held gently, as a fact and not a fear.
If you pray, you can let the line sit inside your prayer.

wordCard.voice: The Garden, what the Quran promises to whoever is kept from the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, after every soul tastes death. Today's word.
